## Code and supply chain security

An agentic harness has a longer supply chain than most services, and several of its links are text rather than code. A typical harness pulls in the Strands Agents framework and its transitive dependencies, a container base image, tool Lambda packages, third-party MCP servers reached through AgentCore Gateway, a model served by Amazon Bedrock, prompts, Cedar policies, a guardrail version, and an evaluation dataset. Any of those can be replaced, poisoned, or quietly changed. The practical approach is to split them into three groups and give each group the control that fits it: code gets scanned and signed, tool definitions get pinned, and model artifacts get inspected when you bring your own.

### Dependency and code scanning in the release pipeline

Agent frameworks move quickly, and their dependency trees are deep. A typical Python agent image pulls in HTTP clients, serialization libraries, OpenTelemetry packages, protocol SDKs for MCP and A2A, and often a vector database client, each with its own transitive dependencies. For container images, including the agent's runtime image and any container-based tool functions, Signer supports signing images in Amazon ECR with the Notation standard, and your deployment pipeline verifies the signature before updating the runtime or function. The effect is that someone who gains write access to an S3 bucket or a Lambda function's configuration can't swap in their own tool code, because the deploy fails signature verification.

### Pinning tool definitions into the harness

Tool descriptions are prompts. The model reads them to decide what to call and how, so a changed description changes behavior exactly like a changed system prompt. That makes MCP rug pulls and description-level poisoning a release engineering problem, and the fix is to treat tool definitions as a pinned, reviewed artifact of the harness.

The pattern has three parts. At build time, the pipeline connects to each Gateway target, lists its tools, canonicalizes the definitions (sorted keys, normalized whitespace), and computes a digest per tool and for the set. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Best MCP Security Tools: Scanners, Gateways, and Registries Worth Running in 2026

Parminder Singh·October 23, 2026·7 min read

The NSA published an MCP security information sheet in June 2026 calling out limited audit logging and weak access controls. The Cloud Security Alliance documented a design-level RCE across every official MCP SDK. MCPTox measured tool-poisoning success rates up to 72% against real servers. This piece sorts the MCP security tooling that actually exists into scanners, gateways, and registries, names what each one covers, and marks which failure modes no HTTP control can reach.

Comparisons & Alternativesai-security agentic-ai llm-security architecture identity-and-authorization cybersecurity

Image: Best MCP Security Tools: Scanners, Gateways, and Registries Worth Running in 2026

The NSA's Artificial Intelligence Security Center published a Cybersecurity Information Sheet on Model Context Protocol in June 2026. Its list of problems includes weak access controls and open-ended serialization. It also names poor approval workflows and token-lifecycle gaps. Separate gaps include limited audit logging and denial-of-service patterns. Its recommendations are equally specific: define trust boundaries and sandbox tool execution. It calls for signed messages and message verification. It also recommends chained-output filters and logs for all tool and model invocations. Two months earlier the Cloud Security Alliance published MCP by Design, documenting OX Security's finding of a design-level remote code execution path across every officially supported MCP SDK, which Anthropic confirmed as intentional behavior of the STDIO interface.

I want to walk through the tools that exist to address this, sorted by what they actually do, and mark clearly which parts of the MCP threat surface no network control reaches.

## TL;DR

Scanners find risky definitions. Gateways enforce policy for remote HTTP traffic. Registries establish provenance before installation. Local execution and workstation compromise need separate controls.

## The three tool categories

MCP security tooling splits cleanly. Scanners inspect servers and tool definitions before or outside runtime. Gateways sit in the traffic path and enforce at call time. Registries establish provenance before installation. Most deployments need one of each, and the common mistake is buying a scanner and believing runtime is covered.

## Scanners and static analysis

mcp-scan (Invariant Labs, now Snyk). The original. It reads MCP config files, connects to servers, pulls tool descriptions, and analyzes them for tool poisoning, MCP rug pulls, and cross-origin escalation. Invariant Labs, an ETH Zurich spin-off, coined both "tool poisoning" and "MCP rug pull" and was acquired by Snyk on June 24, 2025. It also has a `mcp-scan proxy` runtime mode that injects a local gateway to intercept live MCP traffic and apply guardrails entirely on the local machine. Caution before you standardize on it: the tooling appears to be migrating to `snyk/agent-scan`, distributed as `snyk-agent-scan`. Check which repository is canonical before pinning it in CI.

Run `uvx mcp-scan@latest` for a static pass. Its `proxy` mode remains local.

Cisco MCP Scanner (github.com/cisco-ai-defense/mcp-scanner). Open source, announced October 2025. Its distinguishing property is contextual and semantic analysis of tool definitions and implementations rather than pattern matching alone. It runs YARA rules, an LLM-as-judge, or Cisco AI Defense independently or together. Targets tool poisoning and over-privileged tool permissions.

MCP-Shield (github.com/riseandignite/mcp-shield). Scans installed servers for hidden instructions, tool shadowing, behavior modification, exfiltration channels, and cross-origin violations. Worth a correction that several roundups get wrong: this is the work of an independent developer, Nikita Kryzhanouski, inspired by Invariant's research rather than produced by them.

MCP Defender (mcpdefender.com, AGPL-3.0). A desktop application that proxies MCP traffic from Cursor, Claude, VS Code, and Windsurf, checks tool call requests and responses against signatures, and prompts allow or block. It is a local control on a developer workstation, which is exactly why it covers a threat that network tooling never sees, and exactly why it covers nothing about your production agent fleet.

## ToFu Fuzzes 273 MCP Servers and Verifies Bugs in 343 Tools #

Md Nazmul Islam Ananto, Pierre Prevost-Avenel, Colin Smith, Kyungtae Kim, Taegyu Kim and Arslan Khan submitted ToFu: Exploiting and Fuzzing the LLM-Orchestrator-Tool Trust Boundary to arXiv on October 9, 2026. The framework derives semantic security checks from the metadata a tool already publishes, adds a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus, and generates a fuzzing harness and an oracle per tool rather than per server. Run against 273 MCP servers exposing 3,405 tools, it reports 253 verified semantic security bugs in 118 servers, which the abstract counts the other way round as bugs in 343 tools across those same 118 servers. The paper's argument is about the boundary rather than the bug count: the orchestration layer does not enforce the input semantics a tool documents, and arguments the model generated get treated as trusted.

commentary

343 tools whose own schema was decoration, and 253 bugs behind them. The orchestrator is the part that was supposed to enforce the contract, and it is the part that does not.

impact

118 of the 273 open-source MCP servers tested carry at least one tool that does not enforce the input contract it advertises, and 343 individual tools do not. The paper is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

Splunk published SVD-2026-1004 on October 7, 2026 for CVE-2026-76286, affecting Splunk MCP Server below 1.2.1. A user holding `mcp_tool_admin` configures a custom API tool with a destination URL. ## SiYuan's Fifth MCP Advisory Is a Path Guard That Matches Filenames Case-Sensitively #

SiYuan published GHSA-mmgw-3mx9-cfwp on August 21, 2026, later assigned CVE-2026-85580. The advisory's summary states that on Linux the MCP file-access path guard compares a case-variant path against the protected `publishAccess.json` filename using case-sensitive matching, and its details add that a path such as `data/.siyuan/PublishAccess.json` bypasses a case-sensitive basename or suffix comparison "even though the underlying file is the protected metadata file". It does not say how the variant reaches that file. SiYuan shipped a regression test named `TestSecurityReproMCPReadsPublishAccessMetadataOnLinux` and fixed it in v3.8.2 by canonicalising the path and matching with platform-appropriate case semantics. CVSS 6.5. The protected file is the same one CVE-2026-60083 added to the blocklist three weeks earlier.

## The classifier, again

`scan` can send each tool definition to a model you choose and ask whether its text directs the model. It is off by default and advisory unless you pass `--classifier-blocks`. Its prompt changed since last week: it now asks for a concrete violation of authority instead of flagging any imperative, tuned on a synthetic stress set, not on MCPTox.

With `deepseek-flash`  | Rules  | Rules + classifier at `high`
--- | --- | ---
218 held-out MCPTox tools caught  | 171  | 218
45 clean MCPTox servers flagged  | 0  | 0
200 random real servers, blocked or flagged  | 2  | 5
996 sampled packages, blocked or flagged  | 23  | 35

Last week's prompt flagged 147 of the 218 at `high`; this one flags all of them and none of the clean servers. On real servers most of its `high` flags are workflow orders like "call this tool first". It still misses what the rules catch: an injection in a tool's name, a private key asked for as a parameter, `rm -rf ~`. Every classifier run in this comparison together cost about $1.70.

## How it ran, and one thing we broke

Last week the scanners ran on a workstation. This time:

  * Fixed inputs. A manifest with the SHA-256 of every one of the 16,830 input files, written before the runs.
  * Fixed tools. One image for the four other scanners, one for WARDEN, both on the same base. Every installed file matches the package published on npm or PyPI, except the install record pip writes itself. WARDEN was installed from an `npm pack` of the measured commit, byte for byte the 0.16.0 on npm.
  * Isolation. gVisor, no network, a read-only root, 2 GB of memory, one bind mount.
  * Two hosts, one image. The packages were split by a hash of each package's id across two of our servers that run the same image ID. 100 packages ran on both: the five scanners gave identical verdicts and finding codes on both, 100 of 100.

The servers we used are not idle. On one of them a web service hung for about forty minutes while the run was in its heaviest phase, starting eight Node processes at a time under gVisor, and again later. We paused, restarted the service, capped the run at 2 CPUs with the lowest scheduling weight, and reran the 1,193 scans that had timed out instead of answering: 383 on that server, and 810 from the other one, where mcp-audit's fixed 10-second connect window was too short next to our transparency log's own sandbox (800 mcp-audit, 10 mcp-shield). The timeouts were never counted as verdicts.
